{{Short description|American Navy cryptanalyst (1921–2025)}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2025}}
{{For|the soap opera character|Julia Parsons}}
'''Julia Mary Parsons''' ({{née|'''Potter'''}}; March 2, 1921 – April 18, 2025) was an American [[United States Navy|Navy]] [[cryptanalyst]] during [[World War II]], a [[WAVES|WAVE]] and member of a secret all-women team of codebreakers at the [[OP-20-G|Naval Communications Annex]], Washington D.C., now nicknamed the [[Code Girls]],<ref name="Mundy">{{cite book |last=Mundy |first=Liza |author-link=Liza Mundy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vFYRDgAAQBAJ |title=Code Girls: The Untold Story of the American Women Code Breakers of World War II |date=2017 |publisher=[[Grand Central Publishing]] |isbn=9780316352550 |location= |pages= |language= |doi= |jfm= |mr= |zbl= |id= |archive-url= |archive-date=}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=May 2025}} which decrypted enemy naval radio messages.<ref name="NYT">{{cite news |last=Rosenwald |first=Michael S. |date=April 30, 2025 |title=Julia Parsons, U.S. Navy Code Breaker During World War II, Dies at 104 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/30/world/julia-parsons-dead.html |url-access=registration |access-date=May 2, 2025 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |location=New York City, New York |pages= |language=}}</ref><ref name="WashPost">{{cite news |last=Kindy |first=Dave |date=November 11, 2022 |title=She decoded Nazi messages and helped win World War II. Now she's 101 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/history/2022/11/11/julia-parsons-woman-codebreaker-wwii/ |url-access=registration |access-date=May 3, 2025 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |publisher=[[William Lewis (journalist)|William Lewis]] |location=Washington, D.C. |pages= |language=}}</ref> Parsons' section, codenamed "Shark" worked on German Navy [[U-boat]] communications encrypted with the [[Enigma machine]].<ref name="BreakfastClub" /> According to a veteran's group, until her death at the age of 104, she was the last surviving U.S. Navy World War II codebreaker.<ref name="BreakfastClub">{{cite web |last=DePastino |first=Todd |author-link=Todd DePastino |date=March 2025 |title=The Story of WWII Code Breaker and Navy WAVE Julia Parsons |url=https://veteransbreakfastclub.org/code-breaker |accessdate=May 3, 2025 |website=VeteransBreakfastClub.org |publisher= |format= |doi=}}</ref> She was the subject of a local TV documentary,<ref name="WQED">{{cite video |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2ThQVOMGEXY |title=Julia Parsons: World War II Codebreaker tells her story at age 100 |date=November 11, 2021 |medium=Youtube |publisher=[[WQED (TV)|WQED-TV]] |location=Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania |people=}}</ref> honored by a field appearance with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] football team<ref name="Steelers">{{cite video |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uu0wthSALP0&t=72s |title=Julia Parsons Honored by the Steelers |date=4 October 2021 |medium=Youtube |publisher=[[CBS News]] |location= |people=}}</ref> and a 29 March 2024 mention in the [[Congressional Record]].<ref name="Deluzio">{{cite web |last=Deluzio |first=Chris |author-link=Chris Deluzio |date=March 29, 2024 |title=Honoring Ms. Julia Parsons, World War II codebreaker |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CREC-2024-03-29/pdf/CREC-2024-03-29-pt1-PgE291-3.pdf |accessdate=May 3, 2025 |work=[[Congressional Record]], p.E291 |publisher=[[United States House of Representatives]] |format= |doi=}}</ref>

Raised in [[Pittsburgh]], the daughter of Howard G. Potter, a Carnegie Technical School (now [[Carnegie Mellon University]]) teacher, and Margaret (Filbert) Potter, a kindergarten teacher, she graduated 1942 from Carnegie Tech with a degree in humanities.<ref name="NYT" /> She volunteered summer 1942 for the WAVES, and aided by a high school German course was assigned to codebreaking in 1943. At the top-secret Navy codebreaking complex, Parsons and many other women analysts worked six days a week, three shifts per day, with some of the earliest computers, to decipher coded communications with U-boats in the North Atlantic.<ref name="PittsburghPostGazette">{{cite news |date=January 27, 2018 |title=Women in tech across generations: WWII code-breaker shares 'can-do' attitude with aspiring female roboticists |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/education/2018/01/27/World-War-II-codebreaker-women-julia-parsons-robotics-Girls-of-Steel/stories/201801270077 |access-date=May 2, 2025 |newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |publisher=PG Publishing Co. |location=Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania |pages= |language=}}</ref> She met her husband Donald Parsons in the military. After the war, pregnancy ended her naval career and she became a high school English teacher and had three children.<ref name="PittsburghPostGazette" />

Due to her secrecy oath, she did not disclose her wartime codebreaking work to anyone, even her husband and family, until 1997, when she learned it had been declassified in the 1970s.<ref name="NYT" /> From then on, as one of the few surviving veterans of this secret elite World War II occupation, she shared her story with [[Girl Scouts of the USA|Girl Scout]] troops, college robotics clubs,<ref name="PittsburghPostGazette" /> and in a [[Ken Burns]] documentary, was the subject of a TV documentary<ref name="WQED" /> and honored at a field appearance with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].<ref name="Steelers" /> Parsons was thought to be the oldest [[Wordle]] player in the world; her children received her Wordle results daily as a sign that she was still healthy.<ref name="NYT" />
